name: Circuit Breaker
problem: Synchronous failures, excessive latency, or transient timeouts at an outbound dependency cascade backwards: calling threads block, local resource pools fill, and the caller becomes unavailable because its callee is.
forces: An open breaker fails fast at the cost of rejecting calls that might have succeeded.
Per-process breaker state means each node must independently rediscover the same outage.
Threshold calibration — error count, timeout, cooldown — is where the pattern is usually gotten wrong.
solution: Every synchronous call to a component the caller does not own is wrapped in a circuit breaker placed in the outbound infrastructure adapter. A failure in the callee must not cascade into a failure of the caller. Breaker state is shared across the cluster rather than held per process, so one node tripping the breaker propagates immediately to its peers.

appliesTo.guidance: All synchronous inter-module calls implement the breaker; a module failure must not cascade to caller failure. Enforced by DM-R07.
Combined with bulkhead isolation (PAT-0015) and fallback behaviour (PAT-0016) on every inter-service call.
In-process calls have no network failure mode; the breaker applies only to outbound third-party integrations.
Tool invocations that reach external systems are outbound calls and are wrapped identically.

relationships.note: The bulkhead limits how much of the caller one failing dependency can consume; the breaker stops calling it.
An open breaker must return something; the fallback defines what.

governedBy.title: Fault Tolerance and Resiliency Patterns
governedBy.note: The ADR mandates a distributed circuit breaker with cluster-shared state, plus retry with exponential backoff. It does not cover bulkheads or fallbacks.

enforcedBy.statement: All synchronous inter-module calls MUST implement circuit breaker pattern. A module failure MUST NOT cascade to caller failure.

sources.note: DM-R07 rule statement. No prose pattern guide documents this pattern.
